lead: A single-page app loads one HTML file and then swaps views inside the browser. A client-side router connects each URL path to a component, so the back and forward buttons work, and a bookmarked or refreshed URL shows the right view. A refresh does send a request for that path, so the server must be told to return index.html (Section 3). React Router and Angular Router are two implementations of the same idea. You meet this in any dashboard, e-commerce site or admin panel where clicking a product opens a detail view but the page does not blink.
prereq: You need 5.1 for components and 5.2 for state; Unit 1 covers URLs and HTTP requests.

blocks.text: A single-page app (SPA) loads one HTML file. After that, JavaScript builds and replaces the page content. If every click asked the server for a fresh HTML file, the browser would throw away the running app and load everything again. That is slow and it loses state such as a filled form or a scroll position.

A client-side router fixes this. It reads the URL path — the part after the domain, such as /posts/42 — and matches it against a route table. A route is one rule: a path pattern and the component to show. A dynamic segment starts with : and captures one part of the path. The pattern /posts/:id matches /posts/42 and stores 42 under the name id. A wildcard route (written * in React Router and ** in Angular Router) matches any path that no other rule matched, so it usually shows a 404 page.

The router then renders the matched component into a placeholder, called an outlet. When the user clicks a router link, the router changes the URL with the browser's History API and renders the new component. It does not send a new document request. The back and forward buttons still work because the router listens for popstate events.
The figure shows the matching step. The URL is the input; one branch of the component tree is the output.

Install the package with npm install react-router-dom. In main.jsx, wrap the app in BrowserRouter. Inside, declare Routes and Route. In React Router v6 and later, each Route takes path and element. Older versions used Switch in place of Routes and component={Home} or render={() => <Home />} in place of element. Both styles appear in syllabi, so read the version.

blocks.code:
<BrowserRouter>
  <Routes>
    <Route path="/" element={<Home />} />
    <Route path="/posts" element={<PostList />} />
    <Route path="/posts/:id" element={<PostDetail />} />
    <Route path="*" element={<NotFound />} />
  </Routes>
</BrowserRouter>

blocks.text: A child Route written with index (and no path) is the index route, matched at the parent's URL. Nested routes render through <Outlet /> in the parent component. A layout route is a parent Route, with or without its own path, whose only job is to keep shared UI such as a header or sidebar mounted while its children change.

Read /posts/:id with const { id } = useParams(). The value is a string, so convert it before arithmetic. Use <Link to="/posts"> instead of <a href="/posts">. Link calls the router and prevents the browser's normal navigation. NavLink adds an active class when its path matches. After a form submit, call navigate('/posts') from useNavigate(). To redirect during render, return <Navigate to="/login" replace />. A <Route path="*" /> catches every unmatched URL.
Lazy loading keeps the first bundle small: const PostDetail = React.lazy(() => import('./PostDetail')); then render it inside <Suspense fallback={<Loading />}>.

sections.h3: Angular Router and the server rule

blocks.text: Angular declares routes as an array of objects. In a module-based app, import RouterModule.forRoot(routes). In a standalone app, call provideRouter(routes). Each entry has path and either component or loadComponent for lazy loading.

The template puts <router-outlet></router-outlet> where the matched component appears. routerLink replaces href: <a routerLink="/posts" routerLinkActive="active">Posts</a>. The wildcard is '**'. A redirect uses { path: '', redirectTo: '/home', pathMatch: 'full' }. Read the id from ActivatedRoute: this.route.snapshot.paramMap.get('id'). A guard is one line in the route: canActivate: [authGuard].

Two URL modes. History routing uses clean paths such as /posts/42 and needs server help. Hash routing puts the route after #: /#/posts/42. The browser sends only / to the server, so hash routing works on any static host. With history routing, the web server must return index.html for every path that is not a real file. Otherwise a hard refresh of /posts/42 asks the server for a file that does not exist and gets 404. The app never starts. In Express, that fallback is a final route that sends index.html; Express details are in Unit 6.

spec.aria: Six URLs on the left with arrows to four routes on the right: / to Home, /posts to PostList, /posts/42 and /posts/abc to PostDetail, /posts/42/comments and /blog to NotFound.

examples.question: An app declares these routes: / → Home, /posts → PostList, /posts/:id → PostDetail, * → NotFound. The user opens these six paths: /, /posts, /posts/42, /posts/42/comments, /blog, /posts/abc. State the component for each path, and give (a) how many paths reach PostDetail and (b) how many reach NotFound.
steps: / matches the index route exactly, so it renders Home.
/posts matches the /posts rule, so it renders PostList.
/posts/42 has two segments after the domain. The second segment 42 fills :id, so it renders PostDetail. useParams() returns {id: '42'}.
/posts/42/comments has three segments. No rule has three segments, so it does not match /posts/:id. It matches * and renders NotFound.
/blog matches no declared path, so it matches * and renders NotFound.
/posts/abc has two segments after the domain. The second segment abc fills :id, so it renders PostDetail with id 'abc'.
PostDetail count = 2 (paths /posts/42 and /posts/abc). NotFound count = 2 (paths /posts/42/comments and /blog).
examples.answer: PostDetail renders for 2 paths and NotFound renders for 2 paths.

traps: Using <a href="/posts"> instead of <Link to="/posts"> makes the browser fetch the page again, so the app restarts with empty state.
On a hard refresh of /posts/42, the web server must return index.html; otherwise it answers 404 because no such file exists on disk.
Put the wildcard route (* or **) last. If it comes before /posts, it catches /posts and every other URL.
useParams() returns strings. The id for /posts/42 is "42", not the number 42; convert before doing arithmetic.
In Angular, a redirect from the empty path usually needs pathMatch: 'full'; without it the empty path can match every URL and loop.

quiz.a: A rule that maps a URL path to a component. The router renders that component without a full page request.

quiz.q: Why does <a href="/posts"> break a React single-page app while <Link to="/posts"> does not?
quiz.a: The anchor asks the server for a new HTML document, so the app restarts. Link calls the router, changes the URL with the History API and renders the new component in place.

quiz.q: Routes: / → Home, /posts → PostList, /posts/:id → PostDetail, * → NotFound. What renders for /posts/7, and what does useParams() return?
quiz.a: PostDetail renders. useParams() returns {id: '7'}; the value is the string '7'.
NotFound. No route has three segments, so the wildcard '**' matches.

quiz.q: A React app works when you click a Link to /posts/42, but a hard refresh of /posts/42 returns a server 404. Explain the cause and the fix.
quiz.a: The server looks for a file at /posts/42, which does not exist. Add a fallback that returns index.html for every path that is not a real file. Then the app starts and the router reads the URL.

quiz.q: Compare hash routing and history routing for deploying a single-page app.
quiz.a: Hash routing puts the route after #, for example /#/posts/42. The browser sends only / to the server, so it works on any static host. History routing uses clean paths such as /posts/42, but the server must return index.html for those paths or a refresh gives 404.

quiz.q: Which Angular directive marks where the matched component appears?
quiz.a: <router-outlet></router-outlet> (the RouterOutlet directive), placed in the template where the routed component should appear.

quiz.q: After a form submit in React Router, which hook changes the URL from code?
quiz.a: useNavigate(). Call const navigate = useNavigate(); then navigate('/posts') after the submit.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production routers add data loading, error boundaries and code splitting at the route level. Next.js and Remix use file-based routing, where a file path becomes a route. TanStack Router adds typed search parameters. Angular's standalone provideRouter and React Router data routers are the current direction. Search for 'React Router createBrowserRouter', 'Angular router guards' and 'History API pushState'.
